narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Origins are traced to the early 1980s in Japanese clubs and the Takenoko-zoku subculture in Harajuku.
The dance evolved through four distinct popularity booms, with the third boom (1999–2001) being the most significant for international visibility.
on_screen: Map: Japan · East Asia

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Para Para serves as a social, synchronized performance art.
It is performed in clubs, at anime conventions, and in community-organized events.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: File:Parapara dance 2009 France.webm (https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/23/Parapara_dance_2009_France.webm?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=imageinfo&utm_content=original)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Para Para is performed primarily with the arms and hands in synchronized sequences.
Footwork is minimal, usually involving stepping in place or side-to-side, while the upper body executes complex, song-specific choreography.
Watch for Arm sequences.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (nah1-LwkJGQ)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Synchronized group formation, often facing a lead instructor or the front.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is strongly associated with Eurobeat, a fast-paced electronic genre featuring synthesizers and drum machines, originating from European Italo disco and Hi-NRG.
Listen for the Synthesizers, Drum machines.
The pulse is 4/4.
High-tempo electronic music characterized by driving synthesizer melodies and a steady, repetitive kick drum pattern.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key choreographer groups include Shishō Gundan, T-RREX, and Team SEF, who have historically created and taught official routines.
Variants include TechPara (danced to hyper techno) and TraPara (danced to trance).
The dance shares rhythmic similarities with the traditional Japanese Bon Odori, though a direct historical link is not confirmed.

scenes.title: Family tree

Para Para is variant of TechPara: A variant of Para Para danced to hyper techno music.
Para Para is variant of TraPara: A variant of Para Para danced to trance music.

scenes.title: Put it together
